topics.title: Tens and ones
topics.intro: Every number is built from tens and ones, like a race car is built from parts. 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the 3 is worth in 35, and in 53.

topics.title: Number bonds
topics.intro: Number bonds are pairs that make a total. If you know 7 + 3 = 10, you also know 70 + 30 = 100!
topics.teach: Explain how 6 + 4 = 10 helps you work out 60 + 40.
topics.talk: Quick-fire in the car: “I say 7, you say the number that makes 10.”

topics.title: Adding and taking away
topics.intro: Adding and subtracting with bigger numbers: split numbers into tens and ones, and use one fact to check the other.
topics.teach: Explain how you would work out 45 + 27.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to check 36 + 17 = 53 by taking away.

topics.title: Counting patterns, odd and even
topics.intro: Counting in 2s, 3s, 5s and 10s is a superpower for times tables. Spot the rule and you can find any number in a pattern.
topics.teach: Explain how you can tell if a number is odd or even.
topics.talk: Count in 3s together up the stairs.

topics.title: Times tables: 2, 5 and 10
topics.intro: Multiplying is adding equal groups quickly. Dividing is sharing equally, or finding how many groups.
topics.teach: Explain why 3 × 5 is the same as 5 × 3, using an array.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many wheels on 6 racing cars.

topics.title: Halves, quarters and thirds
topics.intro: A fraction is an EQUAL part of something. Two quarters make a half. Three quarters is almost the whole thing.
topics.teach: Explain why a shape cut into 4 unequal pieces is not in quarters.
topics.talk: Cut a sandwich into quarters. How many quarters make a half?

topics.title: Money
topics.intro: Pounds and pence: 100p makes £1. Counting coins is quickest if you start with the biggest.
topics.teach: Explain how to make 75p using the fewest coins.
topics.talk: At the shop, let {him} work out the change from £1.

topics.title: Telling the time
topics.intro: The long hand shows the minutes and the short hand shows the hour. Count in 5s round the clock to read the minutes.
topics.teach: Explain how you know a clock shows quarter to 3.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what time it is on the kitchen clock, then what time it will be in half an hour.

topics.title: Length, mass and capacity
topics.intro: We measure length in centimetres and metres, mass in grams and kilograms, and capacity in millilitres and litres.
topics.teach: Explain which unit you would use to measure a race track, and why.
topics.talk: Guess how many centimetres long a toy car is, then measure it.

topics.title: Pictograms and charts
topics.intro: A pictogram uses pictures to show numbers. Always check the key: sometimes one picture stands for 2!
topics.teach: Explain what half a picture means when one picture stands for 2.
topics.talk: Make a tally of car colours you pass on a walk.

topics.title: Racing, space and hero problems
topics.intro: Word problems hide the maths inside a story. Read carefully, decide what to do first, then check your answer makes sense.
topics.teach: Explain the two steps you would use to solve a problem about racing laps.
topics.talk: Make up a word problem about superheroes for each other.

topics.title: Shapes
topics.intro: Every shape has properties: sides and corners (vertices) for flat shapes, faces, edges and vertices for solid ones.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a cube and a square.
topics.talk: Find a cylinder, a cuboid and a sphere in the kitchen.

topics.title: Time and number facts
topics.intro: Some facts are worth knowing by heart, like how many minutes are in an hour.
topics.teach: Explain how many days are in a week and which day comes after Friday.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many months until {her} birthday.

topics.title: Thinking like a mathematician
topics.intro: Mathematicians ask: is it always true, sometimes true, or never true? Can I prove it? These questions are the real greater-depth challenge.
topics.teach: Explain whether adding two odd numbers ALWAYS gives an even number.
topics.talk: Ask {him}: “Is it always, sometimes or never true that a bigger number has more digits?”

topics.title: Times tables: 3, 4 and 8
topics.intro: The 4 times table is double the 2s, and the 8 times table is double the 4s!
topics.teach: Explain how the 4 times table helps you with the 8 times table.

topics.title: Numbers to 1000
topics.intro: Three-digit numbers have hundreds, tens and ones. 365 is 3 hundreds, 6 tens and 5 ones.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to 299 when you add 1.
topics.talk: Find a three-digit number on a sign and ask what each digit is worth.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting 3-digit numbers
topics.intro: For big numbers, line them up in columns: hundreds, tens, ones. Add or take away one column at a time.
topics.teach: Explain what “carrying” means when you add.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to add two house numbers on your street.

items.prompt: How many sides does a triangle have?
items.explain: Tri means three: 3 sides and 3 corners.

items.prompt: How many sides does a pentagon have?
items.explain: Pent means five.

items.prompt: How many sides does a hexagon have?
items.explain: Hex means six. Bees build hexagons in their honeycomb.

items.prompt: How many sides does an octagon have?
items.explain: Oct means eight, like an octopus with 8 legs.

items.prompt: What is the name of a corner on a shape?
items.explain: A corner is a vertex. More than one are vertices.

items.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?
items.explain: A dice is a cube: 6 square faces.

items.prompt: How many vertices (corners) does a cube have?
items.explain: 4 on the top and 4 on the bottom: 8.

items.prompt: Which 3D shape is like a ball?
items.explain: A sphere is perfectly round with one curved surface.

items.prompt: Which 3D shape is like a tin of beans?
items.explain: Two circle faces and a curved surface.

items.prompt: Which 3D shape is like a traffic cone?
items.explain: A circle face and a point at the top.

items.prompt: A shape has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. What is it?
items.explain: A rectangle also has 4 right angles, but its sides are not all equal.

items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
items.explain: Up and down, across, and both diagonals.

items.prompt: How many minutes are in an hour?
items.explain: The long hand goes all the way round in 60 minutes.

items.prompt: How many hours are in a day?
items.explain: The short hand goes round the clock twice in a day: 2 × 12 = 24.

items.prompt: How many days are in a week?
items.explain: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

items.prompt: How many months are in a year?
items.explain: January to December.

items.prompt: How many minutes are in half an hour?
items.explain: Half of 60 is 30.

items.prompt: How many minutes are in a quarter of an hour?
items.explain: A quarter of 60 is 15.

items.prompt: How many pence are in £1?
How many centimetres are in 1 metre?
items.explain: A metre stick has 100 centimetres.

items.prompt: Which month comes after June?
items.explain: …May, June, July, August…

items.prompt: How many seconds are in a minute?
items.explain: Count to 60 slowly: that is about a minute.

items.prompt: Odd + odd = even. Is that always, sometimes or never true?

options.feedback: Try lots: 1 + 3 = 4, 5 + 7 = 12, 9 + 9 = 18. It works every time.
Try 3 + 5 = 8. That is even!

items.explain: Two odd numbers each have one left over when you pair them up. The two left-overs make a pair, so the total is always even.

items.prompt: A number with more digits is bigger. Always, sometimes or never true (for whole numbers)?

options.feedback: For whole numbers it always works: even the smallest 3-digit number (100) beats the biggest 2-digit number (99).
100 has more digits than 99, and it is bigger.

items.explain: The smallest 3-digit number, 100, is bigger than the biggest 2-digit number, 99.

items.prompt: You can add two numbers in any order and get the same answer. Is the same true for taking away?

options.text: No: 10 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 10

options.feedback: 10 − 3 = 7, but 3 − 10 would go below zero. Order matters for take away.
It does not depend on odd or even: order matters for subtraction.

items.explain: Adding and multiplying can be done in any order. Taking away and dividing cannot.

items.prompt: Turbo says: “34 + 25 = 95.” What mistake did Turbo make?

options.text: Added the tens to the ones in the wrong places: it should be 59

options.feedback: 34 + 25: 3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens; 4 + 5 = 9 ones. 59.
The question is an addition. The mistake is mixing up tens and ones.

items.explain: 3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens. 4 ones + 5 ones = 9 ones. 5 tens and 9 ones is 59, not 95.

items.prompt: {hero} says: “Half of 30 is 13.” How can you prove this is wrong?

options.feedback: Halving makes things smaller. Doubling 30 gives 60.
30 is even, so it halves exactly: 15.

items.explain: To check a half, double it: if it does not give the whole, it is wrong.

items.prompt: Which is greater: {{1/2}} of 20 or {{1/4}} of 48?

options.feedback: Half of 20 is 10. A quarter of 48 is 12. 12 is more.
10 and 12 are not the same.

items.explain: {{1/2}} of 20 = 10. {{1/4}} of 48 = 12. A quarter of a big number can beat a half of a small one.

items.prompt: Which is NOT the same as 4 × 5?

options.feedback: 5 × 4 is the same as 4 × 5: both make 20.
Four fives: 20. This IS the same.

items.explain: 4 + 5 = 9, but 4 × 5 means 4 groups of 5 = 20.

items.prompt: Sparky thinks of a number. When it is shared equally between 2, nothing is left over. What do we know?

options.feedback: Odd numbers always have 1 left over when shared between 2.
Lots of numbers share equally between 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10…

items.explain: Even numbers share equally into 2 with nothing left.

items.prompt: Without working it out exactly: is 48 + 39 closer to 70, 90 or 110?

options.feedback: 48 is nearly 50 and 39 is nearly 40: about 50 + 40 = 90.
Round each number: 50 + 40 = 90.

items.explain: Rounding to the nearest ten gives a quick estimate: 50 + 40 = 90. (The exact answer is 87.)

items.prompt: I am a number between 20 and 30. I am in the 2 times table AND the 5 times table. What am I?

options.feedback: 20 is in both tables, but it is not BETWEEN 20 and 30.
25 is in the 5 times table but it is odd, so not in the 2 times table.

options.text: There is no such number between 20 and 30

items.explain: Numbers in both the 2 and 5 times tables are in the 10 times table: 10, 20, 30… None is strictly between 20 and 30!
